extracted.intended_audience: literate London readers of The Spectator (early 18th-century general public interested in morals, manners, theatre and music)
extracted.subtask_short: moral essays on fame and manners
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical-essay guidance on ambition, reputation, public entertainments (theatre and music), civil salutations, and the art of growing old; presented as prescriptive moral and practical standards for behaviour and cultural production. Intended as advice/readership guidance rather than formal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fame is difficult to obtain and easily lost
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame is a thing difficult to be obtained, and easily lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small slips and infirmities are more conspicuous in a famous man because they are not of a piece with the rest of his character; one false step in momentous concerns breaks ambitious designs. A noble and triumphant merit often overcomes little spots, but a blot of a deeper nature casts a shade on all other beauties. To preserve a great name requires a continual train of noble actions; when fame stands still it flags and languishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small faults harm reputation disproportionately
rubrics_metrics.description: Any little slip is more conspicuous and observable in his conduct than in another's, as it is not of a piece with the rest of his character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such slips contrast with the general character, are industriously proclaimed, and aggravated by others (especially former superiors or equals), they diminish reputation significantly even when minor in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiration is short-lived and must be continually renewed
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiration is a very short-liv'd passion, that immediately decays upon growing familiar with its object, unless it be still fed with fresh discoveries, and kept alive by a new perpetual succession of miracles rising up to its view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even the greatest actions of a celebrated person are expected from him and so, unless continually surpassed by fresh wonders, they cease to enlarge his reputation; fame requires perpetual new actions to survive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fame brings little true happiness and many disquietudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame brings the ambitious man very little happiness, but subjects him to much uneasiness and dissatisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The desire of fame inflames and unsettles the mind, is an object foreign to our nature (no faculty exists to relish it), produces a giddy pleasure that excites fresh desires, and leaves the ambitious often unsatisfied even after attaining fame. Praise can mortify as well as gratify, and silence or insufficient praise causes distress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition is an empty, insatiable good
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambition raises a secret tumult in the soul... It is still reaching after an empty imaginary good, that has not in it the power to abate or satisfy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most other desires can be sated by their proper objects; fame cannot. Many who have as much fame as they desired still thirst after more; therefore ambition is a restless, self-defeating appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fame depends on others' judgment and is precarious
rubrics_metrics.description: The enjoyment of fame is precarious, that it wholly depends on the will of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We are tortured by reproaches, disappointed by silence, and humbled by praise; the absence of fame may make us miserable because we measure loss by imagined value rather than real worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only the Supreme Being can truly judge and reward our merits
rubrics_metrics.description: No other being can make a right judgment of us, and esteem us according to our merits... he that sees every degree of perfection is the only proper judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outward actions are imperfect indicators: many virtues are hidden, some need opportunities to appear, actions may be misinterpreted or arise from contrary principles, and actions cannot show the degree or perfection of internal principles. Therefore seeking human applause is misguided; one should direct desire of fame toward divine approbation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursuit of fame can hinder attainment of ultimate (religious) happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The pursuit after fame may hinder us in the attainment of...that happiness which is reserved for us in another world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three reasons: (1) desire of fame breeds vicious habits; (2) many actions apt to procure fame are not conducive to ultimate happiness; (3) even if actions are instrumental to both ends, if they proceed from desire of fame they fail to attain the last end. Thus motive and final end matter morally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the stage: entertainment should be 'jucunda et idonea dicere vitae' (pleasant and suitable to life)
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of the stage is, as the Latin has it, 'Jucunda et Idonea dicere Vitæ' — pleasant and suitable to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public diversions are necessary to relieve mind and body, but persons of distinction should preside to check what tends to corruption of manners or is too mean for reasonable entertainment; theatrical performances should both please and improve spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre should offer something done as well as said (suitable entertainments for varied audiences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man that goes to a play is not obliged to have either wit or understanding; ... I would have something done as well as said on the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatrical entertainments should provide elements that can instruct or improve those of different capacities (including more physical/display acts), so long as they remain fitting and not corrupting of manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music must express passion/sentiment and heighten poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Musick ... is only valuable, as it is agreeable to, and heightens the purpose of poetry; ... mere musical sounds are... nonsense Verses are in Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music should have some passion or sentiment to express; without that, instruments and voices are little above children's rattles. Composers should aim to aggravate (intensify) what the poetry intends and never present mere sound divorced from meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical proposal standards for concert/opera presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to make a subscription of two guineas, for eight times; that the entertainment, with the names of the authors of the poetry, may be printed, to be sold in the house, with an account of the several authors of the vocal as well as the instrumental musick for each night; the money to be paid at the receipt of the tickets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested operational standards for staging musical entertainments: subscription payment model, printed programs listing poetic and musical authors, sale at the venue; aimed to revive the art, support practitioners' livelihoods, and establish settled notions of music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revival and nationalization of the opera: integrate English poetry with Italian music
rubrics_metrics.description: It was from this opinion... that when Mr. Clayton had finished his studies in Italy, and brought over the opera of Arsinoe, ... they were zealously inclined to assist by their solicitations in introducing so elegant an entertainment as the Italian musick grafted upon English poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocacy for adapting continental musical innovations to English poetic traditions rather than slavishly importing foreign forms; the ideal is to revive music through native literary integration and support English practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outward civilities and salutations should follow common sense and appropriate decorum
rubrics_metrics.description: There are some things which cannot come under certain rules, but which one would think could not need them. Of this kind are outward civilities and salutations ... these ought to be regulated by common sense/right reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe place and time: do not exchange salutations during the Royal Presence or during divine service; avoid ostentatious displays that scandalize others (e.g., showing off in church); salutations should not be forced where refused (preventing aspect) nor be so obsequious as to be inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration for converts and awkward persons in public worship
rubrics_metrics.description: It is worth considering whether, in regard to awkward people with scrupulous consciences, a good Christian of the best air in the world ought not rather to deny herself the opportunity of shewing so many graces, than keep a bashful proselyte without the pale of the church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When outward ceremony or display in religious assemblies may discourage or scandalize prospective adherents (e.g., dissenters, converts), one should temper civility and show restraint to avoid excluding others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art of growing old: value worthy actions over transient pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: You must propose, that no one set his heart upon what is transient; ... the memory of good and worthy actions is a feast which must give a quicker relish to the soul than ever it could possibly taste in the highest enjoyments or jollities of youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To age well, one should avoid squandering life in luxury and wantonness; invest in acts of generosity or public good so that old age brings satisfaction from worthy deeds rather than empty recollections of pleasures. (Practical small comforts—warm night-caps, a cane—are also suggested.)
